pages.x: Ninety years after slavery ended, Black Americans in the South still lived under Jim Crow laws that kept them in separate schools, seats and waiting rooms, and most were stopped from voting. In 1954 the Supreme Court ruled, in Brown v. Board of Education, that separate schools for Black and white children broke the Constitution.

In August 1955 Emmett Till, a 14-year-old boy from Chicago visiting Mississippi, was kidnapped and murdered for supposedly whistling at a white woman. His mother insisted on an open coffin, so the world could see what had been done to him. An all-white jury freed the killers, who later admitted it.

In December 1955 in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus to a white man and was arrested. Black people boycotted the city's buses for over a year, led by a 26-year-old minister, Martin Luther King Jr., until the Supreme Court ruled segregation on buses illegal.

In 1960 four Black students sat down at a whites-only lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and would not leave. Sit-ins spread across the South. In 1961 Black and white Freedom Riders rode buses together into the Deep South; one bus was firebombed, and riders were beaten by mobs.

In Birmingham, Alabama, in 1963, police turned fire hoses and dogs on marching children, and the pictures shocked the nation. That August a quarter of a million people marched on Washington, where King spoke of his dream that his children would one day be judged by the content of their character, not the colour of their skin.

The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned segregation in public places and discrimination at work. In March 1965 state troopers beat peaceful marchers on a bridge in Selma, Alabama, on a day called Bloody Sunday, and months later the Voting Rights Act protected Black Americans' right to vote.

On 4 April 1968 King was shot dead on a motel balcony in Memphis, Tennessee, where he had gone to support striking rubbish collectors. Riots broke out in more than a hundred cities. Malcolm X, who had argued that Black people must defend themselves by any means necessary, had been murdered three years before.

The movement ended legal segregation and won Black Americans the vote in the South, and its peaceful methods inspired movements for the rights of women, gay people and others around the world. But gaps in wealth, housing, policing and justice did not vanish, and the struggle goes on.
